name: SINGAPORE

flag.title: Flag of Singapore
flag.note: Red & white, crescent moon, five stars

lead: Singapore is a tiny island city-state at the tip of the Malay Peninsula — so small you could drive across it in an hour, yet one of the world's wealthiest nations. From a fishing village to a global hub in two generations, it pulses with gleaming towers, fragrant hawker stalls, and rainforest where pangolins still roam the night.
geo: Singapore sits on one main island plus 63 smaller ones at the foot of the Malay Peninsula, hugging the world's busiest shipping lane. There are no mountains — the highest natural point, Bukit Timah Hill, is just 164 metres tall.

With almost no natural resources, Singapore imports nearly all its food and water. Engineers have grown the island by 25% over the past two centuries by pumping in millions of tonnes of sand to reclaim land from the sea.
animals: Singapore is far wilder than its skyline suggests. Smooth-coated otters splash through city canals and have become social-media celebrities. The critically endangered Sunda pangolin — the world's most trafficked mammal — still hides in Bukit Timah and Central Catchment reserves.

Oriental pied hornbills vanished from Singapore by the 1960s but bounced back after conservationists put up nesting boxes. Around 60–100 now soar over parks and roadside trees, a black-and-white bird with an improbably large yellow beak.
culture: Singapore's food is its greatest pride. At hawker centres — giant open-air food halls on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list — Chinese, Malay, Indian, and Peranakan stalls sit side by side. A plate of chicken rice or laksa costs just a few dollars.

Four official languages (English, Malay, Mandarin, Tamil) give rise to a street speech called Singlish, where sentences end with "lah", "leh", or "lor". The national anthem, Majulah Singapura, is sung entirely in Malay.
history: In 1819 British officer Stamford Raffles chose this swampy island as a free-trade port. Within two years traders had flooded in and the population leapt from 150 to 5,000. By 1821, $8 million of goods passed through each year.

Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963 but was expelled just two years later. On 9 August 1965, Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew tearfully announced independence — and built one of the world's richest economies within a single generation.
wows: Changi Airport has won the title of World's Best Airport 14 times at the Skytrax Awards, including 2026.
Singapore has the world's highest GDP per capita by purchasing power parity — richer per person than the USA.
The Night Safari, opened in 1994, was the world's very first zoo designed entirely for nocturnal visits.
Gardens by the Bay's Flower Dome is the world's largest glass greenhouse, certified by Guinness World Records.
Singapore's MRT trains are so precise that delays are officially measured from the five-minute mark.
Despite being tinier than London, Singapore is the world's second-busiest container port by volume.
The country has grown itself over 24% bigger since independence by importing sand and filling in the sea.

myths.myth: You'll be caned for chewing gum
myths.fact: Selling or importing gum is banned (a fine, not caning), but chewing it is not illegal — therapeutic gums from a pharmacist are allowed.

myths.myth: Singapore is just one big mall
myths.fact: Over 300 km of park connectors link nature reserves where otters, hornbills, and even pangolins live wild in the heart of the city.
